text:
## Observations

1. For a fixed second cut \(j\), the suffix contributes the same distinct count for every legal first cut \(i\).
2. If the previous occurrence of \(A_j\) is at position \(p\), appending \(A_j\) increases the middle subarray’s distinct count by one exactly for cuts \(i\) with \(p \le i < j\). Use \(p=0\) when \(A_j\) has no previous occurrence.
3. When the second cut advances to \(j\), the only newly legal first cut is \(i=j-1\). Its middle subarray is empty immediately before \(A_j\) is appended.
4. A lazy segment tree can add one to a contiguous range of cut scores and maintain their maximum at the root.
5. Sweeping \(j\) from \(2\) through \(N-1\) and considering only cuts \(1 \le i < j\) covers every valid split.

## Solution sketch

> For a fixed second cut \(j\), the suffix contributes the same distinct count for every legal first cut \(i\).

1. Precompute the distinct count of every prefix in a left-to-right pass and of every suffix in a right-to-left pass. Use a Boolean array indexed by value, clearing it between passes. During the sweep, add the precomputed suffix count starting at \(j+1\) to the best score for the first two subarrays.

> A lazy segment tree can add one to a contiguous range of cut scores and maintain their maximum at the root.

2. Build a lazy segment tree with one leaf for each possible first cut \(i\) from \(1\) through \(N-2\). Initialize all leaves to negative infinity so that inactive cuts cannot win. After processing position \(j\), each active leaf stores the prefix distinct count through \(i\) plus the middle distinct count from \(i+1\) through \(j\).

> When the second cut advances to \(j\), the only newly legal first cut is \(i=j-1\). Its middle subarray is empty immediately before \(A_j\) is appended.

3. Start the sweep at \(j=2\). Keep an array of last occurrence positions, initialized to zero except for \(A_1\), whose last occurrence is at position \(1\). At each \(j\), activate the leaf for \(i=j-1\) by setting it to the prefix distinct count through \(j-1\). Do this before applying the contribution of \(A_j\).

> If the previous occurrence of \(A_j\) is at position \(p\), appending \(A_j\) increases the middle subarray’s distinct count by one exactly for cuts \(i\) with \(p \le i < j\). Use \(p=0\) when \(A_j\) has no previous occurrence.

4. Read \(p\) from the last-occurrence array and add one to the inclusive leaf range \([\max(1,p),j-1]\). For a cut to the left of \(p\), the previous occurrence is already in the middle subarray. For a cut at or to the right of \(p\), it lies outside the middle subarray. After the update, record \(j\) as the last occurrence of \(A_j\).

> Sweeping \(j\) from \(2\) through \(N-1\) and considering only cuts \(1 \le i < j\) covers every valid split.

5. After each range update, add the suffix count starting at \(j+1\) to the root maximum and keep the largest total. Print that total after the sweep. When \(N=3\), the sweep evaluates exactly one split into three singletons. If every value is equal, the answer is \(3\). If all values are distinct, the answer is \(N\). Preprocessing takes \(O(N)\) time, and each sweep iteration takes \(O(\log N)\) for one point assignment and one range addition. Total time is \(O(N\log N)\), and total space is \(O(N)\).

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
